A salt-laced fog was rolling in, and the fire threw a great, pulsing dome of orange light against it; made the wet sand gleam like polished bronze, just beyond the circle of its warmth; and touched with brief, ghostly fingers the white-painted strakes of the fishing boats drawn up on the shingle, whenever the restless forms moving about the flames allowed the light to escape. Nothing gained more consequence from this uncertain glare than the simple objects of the men's labour, which were transformed into matters of deepest import. There was old Matthew, his face no different than it was at midday, yet in the firelight, with his tangled grey beard and the oilskin hat that had long since molded itself to the shape of his head, he might have been some ancient sea-king presiding over a council of war. There was Mr. Finney, the parson's brother, who had brought down a basket of apples "to keep the chill from the men's bones," as he said; he fussed about with such anxious officiousness, his spectacles flashing, that the leaping shadows made him by turns a worried alchemist or a conspirator counting his gold. Young Jem, tasked with feeding the fire with driftwood, was simply Jem; but when Martha appeared for a moment to bring a jug of water, the light caught the red of her shawl and the strong column of her throat and made of her a smuggler's handsome wife, waiting on the shore. Clara stood for some minutes in the deep shadow of the dory, enjoying the scene, before she stepped into the light, with the same quiet purpose a captain has when she comes upon the quarter-deck to inspect the diligence of her crew. Mr. Finney was at once full of solicitous greetings and hopes that she was not cold, and Matthew gave her a report of the tide. "We'll have a good run on the morrow, miss," he said;--"the water's just right for it; I ain't seen a better set o' the current all season. It turned 'bout an hour past, and the wind's holdin' steady offshore; the fish can't do nothin' but swim right into our nets. I reckon we've mended nigh on forty fathom this evenin'--I'd swear to thirty, anyways. We'd have done more if young Jem here hadn't got hisself tangled in the new hemp--I expect he thought he was a flounder lookin' for a way out." "Now, Mr. Matthew!"--cried Jem, with a grin of good-natured shame. "A truly remarkable industry," declared Mr. Finney, "and the fire provides a most salubrious warmth against the evening miasmas." "Now, Clara," Matthew went on, his blunt fingers working nimbly with a wooden needle, weaving the twine through the broken mesh,--"you understand how this line must be treated once it's spliced?--you got to soak it in the brine tub for a full day, or else it'll be too stiff,--any old brine will do, long as it's salty enough to float an egg; and you let it sit proper; and then when it's taken a good soak--Martha knows about the tarring--you can tell it's ready for the tar when it holds the water but don't feel slimy, and then you got to work the tar in hot, but not so hot it burns the fibre--" "The application of a preservative is, of course, essential," Mr. Finney interjected. "Indeed it is," said Matthew,--"Martha knows the right way--you take a bit o' tallow and mix it in to keep the tar from crackin'--tallow's as good as anything--though I've heard whale oil's better if you can get it clean--" "A distillate of pine resin might prove a more scientifically sound alternative, I imagine," said Mr. Finney. "I have read in a very reputable journal that agitating the fibres gently during the drying process, perhaps by shaking the net periodically, can prevent the strands from adhering to one another." "'Tain't the way of the best net-menders I ever knew," said Matthew; "though I'm not sayin' nothin' against book-learnin', for it's a fine thing in its place; Mr. Abercrombie is a learned man, and his nets are as good as any you'll find; but I hope ours are as good too; and I've seen a fine, supple net that was just left to hang in peace." "You'd be shaking your arms off till morning!" said Jem. Clara listened to it all with a smile, until a figure emerged from the foggy darkness and she found herself beside Mr. Thorne. "I have been enjoying a pipe with your father," he said, "and he gave me leave to seek out the source of all this light and industry. I mean!--not that I required leave, for my curiosity was already quite piqued--" "Ah Mr. Thorne!" said Clara, her laugh a soft note in the night. "You are justly punished for such a formal preamble. But the scene is a compelling one, is it not? I have been watching them for an age." He made no direct reply to her question. "It is a fine sight," said Clara. "If you stand back, by the boat's rudder, Mr. Thorne--does it not look like some ancient rite, with the fog for a curtain and the sea for a backdrop? Look at Jem now with that armful of wood--William! is he not the very image of a boy feeding a signal fire in one of those old border ballads? It has a certain grandeur, does it not, Mr. Thorne?" "I confess," he said with a slight shake of his head, "my imagination is less nimble than yours. I have not once been in your company without being made to see the world through a poet's lens." "That young lady, sir," announced Mr. Finney from across the fire, where he was attempting to spear a hot apple with a pointed stick,--"that young lady, sir, is an inspiration to her--a--to all gentlewomen." "An inspiration!" said Mr. Thorne. "In her appreciation, not her ambition, Mr. Finney means," Clara said in a low voice. "Well I'll not say she ain't a good lass," said Matthew, not looking up from his work,--"she's got a good head on her shoulders--she's as sharp a girl as you'll ever meet!" Nobody could maintain their composure at this, except for Matthew himself, who was wholly absorbed in his craft. "Miss Vance, sir," Mr. Finney continued, his face glowing with earnestness,--"Miss Vance, Mr. Thorne, shows a remarkable dedication to the maritime commerce of our community." "Not by choice alone, I trust?" said Mr. Thorne, his eyes smiling as he asked the question of Clara. But she looked away towards the fire. "You know," she said, a little briskly, pulling her shawl tighter, "I must have a practical mind--with father's health as it is, I am to be a ship owner myself." "So I understand--so your father told me,--but I worry--forgive me--you seem ill-suited to such a weighty enterprise." William sighed, and Clara's eyes met his for a moment in the flickering light.

"Polite," her father mused, a twinkle in his eye. "That is a word that can mean anything or nothing. I spoke with him earlier. He seems a decent enough sort, for a man who has spent his life inland. He does not know a brig from a barque, I'll wager."

She spoke of the firelight, and the earnest debate about knots and nets, and the quaint dignity of the figures in the mist, her voice painting the scene for him as she had seen it. He listened, nodding and smiling, a captain hearing a report from his trusted first mate, content that his ship, for now, was in the safest of hands. And as she spoke, Clara felt the weight of her new duties settle upon her not as a burden, but as a mantle, one she was perhaps more suited to wear than anyone, even she herself, had ever supposed. The poet and the ship owner were not two different people, she began to realize; they were merely two sides of the same coin, minted in the salt and spray of the North Sea coast.

"Admirably, Miss Ringgan, admirably!" the doctor declared, beaming from the other side of the steam. "A testament to the cohesive powers of albumen and farinaceous matter! The patch has vitrified, I believe, under the intense caloric application. It is as sound as the day it was cast!"
"Well, I don't know about all that," said Earl, who had been listening with a skeptical ear while he skimmed the boiling surface. "But it ain't leakin', and that's the main thing. I'll say that for it. Don't know as I'd trust it overnight, but it'll do for the day's work. We've lost a good hour, and the sap's still comin'. Philetus! Don't stand there like a stump! Fetch another turn of wood."
Philetus, who had been gazing at the mended spot with a look of profound wonder, started and trudged off obediently towards the woodpile, his form swallowed by the shadows and then reappearing, laden, in the firelight's glow. The rhythm of the work re-established itself; the scrape of the ladle, the hiss of the sap, the crackle of the fire, the quiet, heavy tread of Philetus, all weaving together into the evening's industry. Fleda took up a smaller ladle and began to help Earl skim the froth from the second, smaller kettle, her movements sure and practiced now. The momentary excitement of the crisis and of Mr. Olmney's presence had passed, leaving behind a steady sense of purpose. The melancholy part of her feelings had receded, while the triumph remained, not as a sharp, bright thing, but as a deep, warm coal glowing within her.
It was not long before Barby appeared again, this time bearing a large basket covered with a checkered cloth. "I figured you'd all be nigh famished," she announced, setting it down on a cleared space on the log barrier. "There's bread and cheese, and some cold ham, and a jug of cider. A body can't live on steam and smoke, no matter how sweet it smells."
The invitation was a welcome one. Earl straightened up with a groan, wiping his brow with the back of a sooty hand. Dr. Quackenboss declared the suggestion "most sagacious," and even Philetus ceased his trudging and drew near, his eyes fixed upon the basket. They gathered around, their faces ruddy and shadowed in the firelight, and took the simple fare from Barby's hands. For a few moments, the only sounds were those of hearty eating.
"That patch is holdin' better'n I thought it would," Earl said, between massive bites of bread and ham. "I do believe we might get this whole run biled down afore we have to quit. And it's a good run; the sap's as sweet as I've seen it in years."
"The meteorological conditions have been most propitious," agreed the doctor, nibbling his cheese with a delicate air. "A fine, crisp frost followed by a generous effusion of solar warmth. The very ideal of the 'sugaring-off' paradigm. As the great Virgil himself noted in his Georgics, 'Frigidus agricolam si quando continet imber'--when the cold rain keeps the farmer indoors, he may--a--prepare many things in advance."
"Well, there ain't been no rain to speak of," said Earl, unimpressed by the citation. "Just good freezin' and good thewin'. That's all you need."
Hugh, who had been leaning against the house, watching Fleda, now spoke. "It has been a successful day, then. In more ways than one. But Fleda, are you certain you are prepared for all of this? This is but one day, and one small victory. Uncle Rolf left things... well, he left them in a state that will require more than a single season's sugar to set right."
Fleda met his concerned gaze without flinching. She had finished her own small portion and was looking into the fire, her thoughts far away. "I am prepared to learn, Hugh," she said softly, but with a new firmness in her voice. "Today has shewn me that much. We found a hole in our most important vessel, a hole that threatened to ruin the best day's work of the season. And we mended it. We mended it with flour and eggs and a bit of ingenuity. If we can do that, what can we not attempt?"
She looked around the circle of faces lit by the fire; Earl's gruff and competent, the Doctor's pompous but good-natured, Philetus's simple and steady, Barby's strong and watchful, Hugh's loyal and anxious. "It is not I who am doing it," she added. "It is we."
A silence fell upon the group, a silence not of awkwardness, but of consideration. Barby nodded slowly. "The girl's got the right of it," she said.
Earl cleared his throat. "Well, talkin' won't pay the taxes. But the sugar'll help. It's a prime lot, this year."
"That Mr. Olmney seems a right thoughtful gentleman," Barby offered, changing the subject as she began to pack her basket. "Rides a fine horse. He stayed a good long spell for a man just out for the air."
"He was rendering a service to science, Barby," said the doctor grandly. "He was a participant in our little empirical demonstration."
"He was stirrin' a pot of goo," said Earl. "Seemed to do it well enough for a man in a fancy coat. I reckon his arms are as tired as Philetus's legs."
At this, a low chuckle was heard from Philetus, a rare and surprising sound, like stones rumbling deep underground. Everyone turned to look at him, but his face had already returned to its usual stolid composure as he chewed the last of his bread.
As the stars began to appear in the darkening sky, the work entered its final phase. The sap in the great kettle had boiled down to a thick, amber syrup, bubbling with slow, heavy "yellow blobbers," just as Earl had described. The air was thick with the rich, cloying scent of maple.
"Alright," Earl announced, "it's time. Fleda, you and the doctor best stand back. Hugh, you and Philetus, give me a hand here. We got to strain this into the coolin' cask."
The next part of the operation was a heavy and precarious one. With great care, using long poles looped through the kettle's handles, the four men lifted the huge iron vessel from its hooks over the fire. Steam billowed out, momentarily obscuring them in a hot, sweet-smelling cloud. They moved with slow, shuffling steps to a large wooden tub that had been set nearby, over which Barby and Fleda had stretched a clean woollen cloth.
"Easy now, easy," Earl grunted. "Let her down slow... now, tip her. Not too fast!"
A thick, golden-brown river poured from the kettle's lip, through the cloth, and into the tub below, steaming and glowing in the firelight. Fleda watched, mesmerized. It was the culmination of the day, the tangible, liquid treasure for which they had all laboured. It was more than just sugar; it was firewood and flour, lamp oil and taxes, a defence against the coming year's uncertainties. It was hope, clarified and boiled down.
When the last of the syrup had been drained, and the heavy kettle set aside to cool, a collective sigh of a different sort went through the group; a sigh of accomplishment and weariness. The fire was banked, the tools gathered. The day's sugaring was done.
Fleda walked back towards the house beside Hugh, her boots crunching on the freezing snow. The air was sharp and cold now, a clean contrast to the smoky heat of the fire. Every muscle in her back and arms ached with a dull, unfamiliar pain.
"He was right, you know," Hugh said quietly, breaking the companionable silence. "Mr. Olmney. It is a great burden you are taking on."
"It is," Fleda agreed, looking up at the vast, starry sky. "But it is my own. And tonight... tonight it does not feel quite so heavy. It feels earned. There is a difference."
"There is," he said. He hesitated, then went on. "What do you truly know of him, Fleda? Of Mr. Olmney?"
"I know he is a friend of Mrs. Rossitur's cousin," she answered simply. "I know he is a gentleman, and that he is not afraid to get his coat dirty. And I know that he understands things without having to be told them."
"He is lately returned from Europe, I hear," Hugh supplied. "He is very wealthy. Old family, new money, some combination of the two. No one seems quite sure. They say he bought The Eyrie for a whim, and may sell it on another."
"I see," Fleda said, though she was not sure that she did. The man who had spoken so earnestly about her 'great work' did not seem like a man of whims. The memory of his steady gaze as he stirred the flour and eggs was a solid and reassuring thing.
They reached the kitchen door, where the warm light of a lamp spilled out onto the snow. Inside, Mrs. Rossitur was waiting, a look of gentle anxiety on her face.
"My dear child," she exclaimed, coming forward to take Fleda's cold hands. "You must be utterly spent. But your eyes are so bright!"
"We are victorious, Mrs. Rossitur," Fleda announced, a weary smile touching her lips. "The great kettle is mended, and the syrup is strained and settling. Earl says it is one of the best runs in years."
"Thank heavens," the older woman breathed. "I have been picturing all manner of disasters. And Mr. Olmney? He came back with Hugh. Did he... find our little operation amusing?"
"He found it instructive," Fleda replied, unbuttoning her smoke-scented coat. "He was a great help to us, in fact. He is a most... capable man."
Mrs. Rossitur's soft eyes twinkled. "So I have always heard. It was very kind of him to stay and offer his assistance. Very kind indeed."
Later, alone in her own room, Fleda stood before the small looking-glass. The girl who looked back at her was a stranger. Her hair was tousled and smelled of woodsmoke, a smudge of soot was traced high on one cheekbone, and her face was flushed not with the heat of a ballroom but with that of an open fire. She held up her hands. They were chapped from the cold and reddened from work, with a small, clean blister forming on her right palm where the ladle had rubbed. These were not the hands of the young lady who had arrived at her uncle's farm only a few months before, a young lady whose chief concerns had been new sheet music and the proper shade of a ribbon.
She thought of Mr. Olmney's parting words. 'You are undertaking a great work here.' He had seen it. He had not seen a young woman of elegant advantages playing at being a farmeress, as Dr. Quackenboss had put it; he had seen the work itself, and the burden of it, and the dignity within it. 'Do not let the burden of it overwhelm you.' The words were a caution, but they had felt like an encouragement, a statement of faith. He believed she was capable of bearing it.
The ache in her shoulders was a dull, heavy reality. The figures she had run with Hugh the night before, the debts and the mortgages and the lean state of the larder, were a stark and frightening truth. The burden was immense. And yet, as she blew out her candle and slid between the cold, clean sheets, she felt a profound sense of peace. The day had been won. The syrup was cooling in the cask. And she was no longer facing the vastness of her task entirely alone. A strange and quiet hope, as sweet and substantial as the night's harvest, began to grain within her heart.
